source.book: Reading & Writing Farsi (Persian): A Workbook for Self-Study

units.title: Orientation & the Sound System
units.goal: Produce the four sounds English doesn't have (kh, zh, gh, ein), hear how much flatter Farsi stress is than English, and recognize when the book is showing formal vs. colloquial forms.

lessons.title: The Sound System
objectives: Hear kh, zh, gh, and ein without trying to read anything yet
Notice where each sound is made in the mouth compared to its nearest English sound

tasks.text: Play track I-01 straight through once, just listening for the four sounds — don't try to write anything yet.
Read the pronunciation notes on pages 5-7 for how kh, zh, gh, and ein are each formed.
Say each of the four sounds out loud several times, comparing your version against the audio.
Say all four sounds back to back and check that they're clearly distinguishable from each other, not blurring together.
Without looking at the page, say all four sounds again from memory, in any order.

lessons.title: Stress & Rhythm
objectives: Notice that Farsi stress is flatter and more even than English's strong-syllable stress
Catch yourself over-stressing syllables out of English habit, and correct it

tasks.text: Listen to a short phrase from the intro material and pay attention to how evenly the syllables land, compared to English.
Read the note on stress/rhythm on page 7-8.
Say the same phrase back twice: once with English-style stress, once flattened out. Notice the difference.
Pick any short phrase from the page and say it three times, deliberately flattening the stress a little more each time.
Say the phrase once more from memory, aiming for the flatter rhythm without thinking about it.

lessons.title: Formal vs. Colloquial
objectives: Recognize the book's notation for formal (written/polite) vs. colloquial (spoken) Farsi
Understand why this distinction matters before starting on vocabulary

tasks.text: Read pages 9-10 on formal vs. colloquial Farsi and how the book marks the difference.
Find the example pair(s) of a formal and colloquial version of the same word or phrase, and note what changes between them.
If audio is available for the examples, listen for how the colloquial version sounds shortened or softened compared to the formal one.
Write one sentence, in your own words, explaining when you'd expect to hear the colloquial form vs. see the formal one.
Quiz yourself: given a formal-looking word, guess whether its colloquial form would be longer or shorter, then check.

units.title: Vowels, Consonants & Numbers
units.goal: Name every vowel type in the Farsi vowel system, and read and write the Farsi numerals 0-9 and multi-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Short Vowels
objectives: Name each short vowel and recognize its written mark
Hear each short vowel in isolation

tasks.text: Play track A01-01 and listen for each short vowel sound in isolation.
Read pages 11-12 and learn the name and written mark for each short vowel.
Copy each short-vowel mark a few times, on its own, to get the shape into your hand.
Say each short vowel out loud while writing its mark, matching sound to shape.
Cover the page and name all the short vowels from memory, in order.

bookPages.title: Farsi Vowels — Long and Short
instructions: Read the page through once without stopping to memorize anything.
Play audio A01-01 and listen to the three long vowels while following along with the page.
Say each long vowel out loud alongside the audio, three times each.
Note that the long vowels have their own letters, while the short vowels are marks placed above or below a letter — this distinction matters for everything that follows.
Move on when you can hear the difference between the long and short version of the same vowel.

bookPages.title: Short Vowels, Shared Consonants, and Sounds New to English
instructions: Play A01-02 and listen to the remaining short vowel examples.
Read the consonant list — these are the sounds you already own from English, so they cost you nothing to learn. Skim, don't drill.
Slow down for the second half of the page: the sounds that don't exist in English. These are the ones worth real time.
Play A01-03 and repeat each unfamiliar sound out loud until your mouth can find it without thinking.
Pay attention to the reading tip about z and s — treating them as interchangeable is a habit English speakers bring in and have to unlearn.

lessons.title: Long Vowels & Diphthongs
objectives: Name each long vowel and diphthong
Hear the difference between a short and a long vowel

tasks.text: Play track A01-02 and listen for the long vowels and diphthongs.
Read pages 13-14 and learn the name and written form of each long vowel and diphthong.
Copy each long-vowel/diphthong form a few times.
Say a short vowel then its long counterpart back to back, several times, to feel the length difference.
From memory, list every vowel type covered so far — short, long, and diphthong.

bookPages.title: Overview of the Farsi Alphabet (Part 1)
instructions: This is a reference table, not something to memorize in one sitting. Treat it as a map you'll come back to.
Play A01-04 and go down the table row by row, listening and reading at the same time.
Notice the rows with multiple characters sharing one sound — those groups are the main thing that makes Farsi spelling tricky, so flag them mentally now.
Cover the Sound column and try to produce the sound from the character alone. Do one pass, note what you missed, move on.
Don't chase mastery here. You'll see every one of these letters again in detail in Section 2.

lessons.title: Consonant Overview
objectives: Get a first look at the full consonant set before learning individual letters
Notice which consonants look similar and will need extra care to tell apart

tasks.text: Play track A01-03 and just listen to the consonant set read aloud once through.
Skim pages 14-15's consonant chart — don't try to memorize it yet, just get oriented.
Pick out three consonants that look visually similar to you and jot down what distinguishes them (dots, position, etc.).

bookPages.title: Writing Rules — Tracing Farsi Numbers 0–6
instructions: Grab your practice notebook before starting — you write these in the notebook, not in the book.
Look at the small numbered arrows on each digit. Those are the stroke order: number 1 is where your pencil starts, number 2 is the next stroke, and so on.
Copy each digit slowly, one full line per digit, following the arrows exactly. Speed comes later; the stroke order is the thing you're actually installing right now.
Say the digit's value out loud as you write it so the shape and the meaning bind together.
If a digit feels awkward, that usually means you're drawing it rather than writing it — go back and check you're starting at arrow 1.

lessons.title: Farsi Numerals 0-9
objectives: Recognize and write each Farsi numeral 0-9
Say each numeral aloud correctly

tasks.text: Play track A01-04 and listen to the numerals 0-9 read aloud in order.
Read pages 16-17 and learn the written form of each numeral 0-9.
Write the numerals 0-9 in order, then again out of order from a self-made shuffled list.
Say each numeral out loud as you write it.
Have someone (or a random-number generator) call out digits 0-9 and write each one down as fast as you can.

bookPages.title: Tracing 7–9, and Reading Numbers Aloud
instructions: Finish the tracing practice for the last few digits in your notebook, same method as page 15.
Switch to the reading half of the page. Now you're learning the spoken names, not the shapes.
Play A01-05 and repeat each number name out loud. The names for 1 through 20 have to be memorized; past that, the system becomes predictable.
Take the reading tip seriously — the romanized spellings are a crutch to get you started, not a pronunciation guide. Reading them silently will teach you the wrong sounds.
Self-check: count 0 to 10 out loud from memory, then write the digits for a few numbers a friend or a random number generator gives you.

bookPages.title: Exercise 1.1 and 1.2 — Listening and Transcribing Numbers
instructions: Set up first: notebook open, headphones in, audio queued. Write answers in the notebook so the book stays clean and you can retake this later.
Exercise 1.1 — play A01-06 and pick the option matching the number you hear. Number your notebook 1 through 6 to match.
Exercise 1.2 — play A01-07 and write what you hear as Farsi digits, not English ones. This is the harder half; it tests shape recall and listening at the same time.
Allow yourself one replay per item, then commit to an answer. Endless replaying turns a test into a listening exercise and hides what you actually know.
Check against the answer key on the publisher's site. Anything you missed, go back to page 16 and redrill just that number.
Passing bar before moving to Section 2: you can hear any digit 0 through 10 and write it correctly on the first listen.

lessons.title: Reading Multi-Digit Numbers
objectives: Read a multi-digit Farsi number left-to-right the way the book explains it
Write a multi-digit number from a spoken or English-numeral prompt

tasks.text: Play track A01-05 and listen to a few multi-digit numbers read aloud.
Read pages 17-18 on how multi-digit numbers are written and ordered.
Write out today's date and your phone number using Farsi numerals.
Convert five two- or three-digit English numbers of your choosing into Farsi numerals.
Read your own written numbers back out loud without hesitating.

units.title: First Letters
units.goal: Read and write Alef, Be, Noon, Daal, Re, long A (آ), Meem, and Seen; greet someone in Farsi; recognize basic subject-verb-object word order.

lessons.title: Letter — Alef (ا)
objectives: Recognize Alef in isolated and connecting positions
Write Alef cleanly from memory

tasks.text: Play track A02-01 and listen for how Alef sounds.
Read pages 20-21 and learn Alef's isolated and connecting forms.
Trace Alef a few times, then write it freehand until it's consistent.
Write Alef five times in a row without looking at the page.
Say Alef's sound while writing it, once more, from memory.

lessons.title: Letter — Be (ب)
objectives: Recognize Be's isolated, initial, medial, and final forms
Write the first real Farsi word using Be and Alef

tasks.text: Play track A02-02 and listen for how Be sounds.
Read pages 21-22 and learn Be's four written forms.
Trace, then freehand, all four forms of Be.
Write بابا (bâbâ — dad) using Be and Alef, the two letters you now know.
Write Be's four forms from memory, unprompted.

lessons.title: Letter — Noon (ن)
objectives: Recognize Noon's four written forms
Read/write a real word combining Noon and Alef

tasks.text: Play track A02-03 and listen for how Noon sounds.
Read pages 22-23 and learn Noon's four written forms.
Trace, then freehand, all four forms of Noon.
Write نان (nân — bread) using Noon and Alef.
Write Noon's four forms from memory.

lessons.title: Letter — Daal (د)
objectives: Recognize Daal (a non-connecting letter) in context
Read/write a real word combining Daal and Be

tasks.text: Play track A02-04 and listen for how Daal sounds.
Read pages 23-24 — note that Daal doesn't connect to the letter after it, unlike Be and Noon.
Trace, then freehand, Daal's isolated and final forms.
Write بد (bad — bad) using Be and Daal.
Write Daal from memory and explain out loud why it doesn't connect forward.

lessons.title: Letter — Re (ر)
objectives: Recognize Re (also non-connecting) and tell it apart from Daal
Read/write a real word combining Daal and Re

tasks.text: Play track A02-05 and listen for how Re sounds.
Read pages 24-25 and compare Re's shape against Daal's — they're easy to confuse at first.
Trace, then freehand, Re, then alternate writing Daal/Re pairs to drill the difference.
Write در (dar — door / in) using Daal and Re.
Write five letters in a row, mixing Daal and Re at random, and check you got each one right.

lessons.title: Letter — Long A (آ, Alef with Madda)
objectives: Recognize آ as the long-A carrier, distinct from plain Alef
Read/write a real word using آ and Be

tasks.text: Play track A02-06 and listen for the long-A sound.
Read pages 25-26 on آ and how it differs from a plain Alef.
Trace, then freehand, آ a few times.
Write آب (âb — water) using آ and Be.
Write آ and ا side by side from memory and say the sound difference out loud.

lessons.title: Letter — Meem (م)
objectives: Recognize Meem's four forms
Read/write a real word combining everything learned so far

tasks.text: Play track A02-07 and listen for how Meem sounds.
Read pages 26-27 and learn Meem's four written forms.
Trace, then freehand, all four forms of Meem.
Write مادر (mâdar — mother) using Meem, Alef, Daal, and Re.
Write Meem's four forms from memory.

lessons.title: Letter — Seen (س)
objectives: Recognize Seen's four forms — the last new letter of the unit
Read/write a real word combining Seen with earlier letters

tasks.text: Play track A02-08 and listen for how Seen sounds.
Read pages 27-28 and learn Seen's four written forms.
Trace, then freehand, all four forms of Seen.
Write سرد (sard — cold) using Seen, Re, and Daal.
Write all eight letters learned in this unit, in order, from memory.

lessons.title: Greetings
objectives: Read and say a basic greeting and its reply
Notice which greeting words use letters you've already learned

tasks.text: Read pages 28-29 and 131 for the basic greeting phrases the book introduces here.
Say each greeting phrase out loud a few times.
Practice a short back-and-forth: greet, then give the reply, out loud, without reading it.
Write down one greeting and its reply from memory.

lessons.title: Basic Sentence Order (Subject–Verb–Object)
objectives: Identify subject, verb, and object in a simple Farsi sentence
Notice that Farsi verb order differs from English

tasks.text: Read pages 29-30 and 131-132 on basic sentence word order.
Find one example sentence and label which part is the subject, which is the verb, and which is the object.
Write one simple sentence of your own following the same subject-object-verb pattern, using letters you already know where possible.
Say your sentence out loud.
Explain out loud, in your own words, how Farsi word order differs from English word order.

lessons.title: Unit 3 Review & Reading Practice
objectives: Read a short passage using only Unit 3's eight letters
Confirm all eight letters are solid before the checkpoint

tasks.text: Read the practice text on pages 32-34, sounding out each word letter by letter where needed.
Copy out two or three words from the passage by hand.
Go back through all eight letters from this unit and write each one's four forms once more.
Note which of the eight letters still feels shakiest, and plan to spend extra review time on it.

units.title: Building Words
units.goal: Read and write Te, Ze, E, Kaaf, Ee, Ye, and Oo; use personal pronouns; form plurals.

units.title: People & Things
units.goal: Read and write Pe, Sheen, Fe, O, Gaaf, and Ghaaf; learn family vocabulary; use this/that.

units.title: Describing
units.goal: Read and write Khe, Che, He (ه), Jeem, Laam, Vaav, and Khaa; use adjectives and ezâfe; learn body and weather vocabulary.

units.title: Out in the World
units.goal: Read and write Zhe, Saad, He (ح), Zaad, Taa, and Zaa; use prepositions; learn grocery and restaurant vocabulary.

units.title: Verbs
units.goal: Read and write Ein, Ghein, Se, and Zaal; conjugate present-tense verbs from their stems.

units.title: Marks & Questions
units.goal: Read and write tashdeed, hamze, and tanveen; form WH questions; learn animal vocabulary.

units.title: Reading for Real
units.goal: Read the geography passages aloud, review all four sections, and read unvowelled Farsi text — the actual finish line, since real Farsi mostly drops the diacritics beginners rely on.
